utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before I ask Mr. Oric whether he is following, I mean see on my monitor here "Upon commencing at 9.38 a.m." I mean, for the record purposes, it goes to our advantage, but it doesn't reflect the truth. So, yes, Mr. Oric, can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour, ladies and gentlemen. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down, and good morning to you. Appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, and also good morning to the Defence team. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution. I'm here together with co-counsel, Ms. Patricia Sellers, Ms. Joanne Richardson, and our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink. And later on this session, also Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio will join the team.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Jones is glad to hear that. Thank you, and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the colleagues from the Prosecution. I'm Vasvija Vidovic and together with Mr. John Jones, I represent the defence of Mr. Naser Oric. We are joined by our legal assistant Ms. Cosic and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, and good morning to you and your team. Any preliminaries? Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. With a view to the submissions to put to this Trial Chamber later on this session, I would like to inform you that we will not make use of jurisprudence and the issue, related issue, of the public domain, and I already updated Defence in that respect. And also I -- the second is that I have a request not to close the direct examination of this witness today until we are able to update you of the outcome of the search of the background of this person Slobodan Misic, as we are ongoing that from yesterday afternoon. So that can be still included in the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. I appreciate your intervention, Mr. Wubben. And I don't think it calls for any remarks from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, just so I understand, I take it that means I'll conclude my examination-in-chief, the Prosecution will start their cross-examination, but I'll have leave to reopen on that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's how I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. If I may. My suggestion was not to close, not to close the examination-in-chief, but wait for this final outcome of the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. So let's -- let me say whether I have understood you well. It means basically that when, after, say, an hour from now, Mr. Jones finishes with his examination-in-chief, you will not start the cross-examination immediately, but you will -- you are asking for us to wait until we get a feedback from you on your findings relating to Slobodan Misic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then it seems that you would require us to turn again towards your direction to see whether you have any further questions to put to the witness, following which, if there are, then we will start with the cross-examination. Of course, it also means that you will have a right to re-examine the witness in any case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. My concern is then naturally for this witness and for how long he's going to be in The Hague, because at this stage obviously -- well, I appreciate obviously there was urgent business this morning of Your Honour Judge Eser which obviously couldn't wait and so we've started a bit late already. But as it is, if then after my examination-in-chief there's even further delay, I fear this witness may not be finished by this week and he'll have to stay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but we will -- if necessary, you know, we have a very long weekend, actually, Mr. Jones. And basically, at that point in time, I would rather you finish your in chief, we send him home, make sure that he is left incommunicado in some way or another, have some kind of control over him, and then we bring him back, if necessary, when we need to start with the cross-examination. Yes, Ms. Vidovic. Otherwise he will have to stay over the long weekend.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd just like to appeal to you to keep in mind the fact that both of this witness's parents are disabled and he had huge difficulties in getting here. I really don't know how we can swing it again, because it's a huge problem for him. I really don't see why the Prosecutor can't start the cross-examination, and then in case any further evidence crops up, we can reopen the examination-in-chief. I don't see any legal obstacles to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, let's -- yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are confident that the cross-examination will be finalised by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On Friday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: By Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: By Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Well, we will try to aim for Thursday, but it might -- should at least be on Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I have full confidence in your cooperation, both of you. I mean -- so I look at this optimistically, let's put it like that, at least from what I have just heard. So let's not lose more time, unless there are any further issues that you would like to raise --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see none. So let's start with the witness. If it seems that what I'm going to announce enjoys the consensus of everyone -- so if it does not, if anyone does not agree with it, please let me know now. The idea is that we will now -- that we have started, will go until 12.20, 12.20; then we will have one break of 30 minutes, from 12.20 to 12.50; then we'll start, it means, at 12.50 and we'll finish at 14.35, if that is agreeable to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think the parties would agree to that, my staff and the rest, I know that they agree. What I want is thumbs up from the interpreters' booths. Yeah.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is all right with the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The recorder, is it all right with you? Okay. Thank you. The technicians -- it's very hard to -- okay. It seems to be -- yeah, they are waving, too. It seems to be all right. So that's -- will be our schedule, and I thank the cooperation of everyone. I thank everyone for your cooperation. Yes, you can bring the witness in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, good morning to you. Good morning, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hope you've had enough time to rest. We are going to continue. We started a little bit later because one of us had a prior important engagement that he had to attend to, but now we can start and we can continue. And we hope to be able to finish with you tomorrow or, if things go wrong, at the latest, on Friday. So, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Jones: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And apologies from me to Mr. Alic that you had to wait 45 minutes this morning. I didn't hear a response, but I trust the equipment will be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you recall, Mr. Alic, that yesterday when we left of we were looking at an article referring to a volunteer called Slobodan Misic and his activities in the Drina area. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have a new exhibit in that regard, which has already been distributed. For the record, it's the article which the headline is "I keep dreaming about snakes drinking blood." And the date is 8 November, 1997, in the publication "Fokus" and the ERN for the record is 00659264 to 00659269.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'll just read the introduction. You have it in front of you. "Misic was arrested by the Serbian secret police in the Editorial Office of the Vranjski Novine. The Dnevni Telegraf published his confession, warning its readers about atrocities mentioned in the text." And it says: "From the correspondent of Dnevni Avaz, Podgorica." Firstly, can you tell us where Podgorica is?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podgorica is in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And it says: "Two days ago, members of the Serbian secret police arrested Slobodan Misic, Top, the Serbian volunteer whose confession about the crimes in Bosnia and Herzegovina have been published in the Vranjski Novine newspaper. He was arrested in their editorial office. Vukasin Obradovic, editor of the Vranjski Novine, said that Misic was arrested by three members of the Serbian State Security Service. "In addition to this, they seized tapes of the interview and Misic's authorised transcript." And then I move down -- first of all, do you recall Slobodan Misic as being the name of the individual in the article yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read where in English it's 00659267. One moment, please. Of course, I'm -- there's only an English version, I appreciate, but it's being interpreted for the witness, which is what counts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't envisage a problem, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And so I'll read: "In Bosnia, I was on the bank of the Drina. We held the corridor from Skelani to Bratunac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure that he has found the -- that he is receiving, in other words, interpretation, since he hasn't got the text of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you receiving interpretation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones is reading from this document now, so it's important that you follow precisely what is being translated to you. Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you please --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'll read slowly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- read slowly --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- so that the interpreters can catch up completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "In Bosnia, I was on the bank of the Drina. We held the corridor from Skelani to Bratunac. Frankly speaking, we had everything: Food, weaponry, and ammunition. We fought against Muslims, poor and hungry lot. We guarded Serbian villages from their intrusion. They came to steal food to be able to survive. I watched one of them voraciously eating a corn-cob. I let him finish and then I cut his throat and into the Drina he goes. We would round them up from ambush from time to time; we would go to cleanse Muslim villages in the hills." And first of all, pausing there, what I've just read to you, does that correspond with your experiences in the area, namely, that the Serbs had everything, that the Muslims were poor and hungry, and that they were killed by Serbs in ambushes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that Muslim villages in the hills were cleansed by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, except for the villages of Jagodnja and Joseva, that is to say, the part of Jagodnja which had not been set on fire, it was in 1992. And all the other villages in the hills had been cleansed on the part of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then moving on: "Decapitated bodies. We were the Territorial Defence but special units used to come too. The Red Berets in camouflage uniforms, a company of some 30 people, to lead us volunteers. I don't know who they were. They were not Arkan's men. They were not Seselj's men. I didn't even dare ask. We attack, burn, kill, capture a few people, and we get back. We would capture women and children. We did not rape women, but they were killed too." I'll stop there. Now, I asked you already about the Territorial Defence in Fakovici. You recall your testimony as far as that was concerned?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you aware, too, in 1992 in this area of other units, special units in the area, in addition to the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've told us how Muslim women were killed in Jagodnja and Joseva in May 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One final thing on this article. At the bottom it says: "I remember when I cut that Muslim's head off and threw it into the Drina. Although it was cold, dozens of snakes suddenly gathered around him to drink blood." My question about this is simply: That detail is not something, is it, that we saw in the article yesterday, this detail about the snakes?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is additional information in this document that we didn't see yesterday?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't see that yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones. This document which, which is entirely in English, consists of six pages, with ERN 00659264 right through and inclusive of 00659269, is being tendered, received, marked, as Defence Exhibit D833.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Now, with the usher's assistance, we have some further documents, starting with one with the ERN 04359976, slightly out of the sequence I planned before. We should be able to follow. And for the record, I'll just read the document. The date is 29 October 1992, request for finance to be paid to the account Skelani TO, Territorial Defence, payment of salary to fighters from Fakovici, Radijevici, paid on 29 October 1992, Radijevici Platoon Commander Miki.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this refers to fighters from Fakovici and Radijevici, but you agree, do you not, that it's signed by a platoon commander?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you told us yesterday how, on the 5th of October, 1992, Serb soldiers were shooting from houses in Radijevici. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've told us how Fakovici was linked to Skelani. Does that also apply to Radijevici? Was that linked to Skelani?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As I said, from Bjelovac to Skelani and further down, it was the municipality of Skelani which had been set up, including Jagodnja and Joseva. So Ognjen Markovic said that in the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Could I have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. This document which consists of two pages, one -- the original being in B/C/S, with ERN number 04359976 and the other is a corresponding translation thereof into English is being tendered, marked, and received as Defence Exhibit D834.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And now the next document is ERN 04359975. And again, for the record, it says: "Republika Srpska, Skelani municipality, municipal department of the Ministry of Defence." And the date is 14 November 1992. And it says "Payment of LD, personal income, for August." And then it says: "Fakovici, Radijevici." I'll give you a moment to look at that. Now, you'll recall in the last document we saw payment of salary to fighters from Fakovici, Radijevici. This document just says: "Fakovici, Radijevici." Can you explain this personal income, LD? Is that something which is paid to a village or is it paid to individuals?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was paid to individuals who were members of the armed forces. It was the soldiers' pay, for the soldiers who were in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And this refers to August. It's a payment, obviously, which is signed November 1992. But that would refer to August 1992, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that Defence counsel has given the answer within the question. This is something that refers to August, so that -- and then he asked the witness, Mr. Alic: Does it refer to August? So I find that there is an answer that's been presumed. Certainly Mr. Alic might answer in the same manner or in a different manner, but so that that's clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think partly you are right, Ms. Sellers; but on the other hand, you have a document which is dated the 14th of November, which refers to a payment accountable to August, and basically it consists of an alleged payment. In other words, we have a payment being effected in November. And the witness is being asked to confirm that basically this is a payment which is being effected in November but which refers to the salaries that were due for the month of August. That's how I understand it. And if he doesn't agree with that, he will just say "I don't agree" or "I read it differently." But it's true that the question contains partly --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It's really this, Your Honour. It's so obvious that perhaps I don't need to put the question. It's November 1992, it's for August --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You might as well do without the question. But if the witness wants to answer it, of course he can.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll put it this way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What year do you think that refers to, August? August of what year?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The last thing I require is to have the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I love the sound of the Serbo-Croat language, but I prefer to be able to follow in English today. The problem is technical, obviously. I'm receiving translation of what I am saying into Serbo-Croat. So while that is being taken care of, I am going to mark -- enter and mark this document, this document which consists of two pages, one in Serbo-Croat, which bears ERN 04359975, and then the equivalent translation thereof into English being the second page is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D835. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And the next exhibit just in this sequence we have is 04359974. I'm actually tempted to tender them together. You'll see the similarity. But I'll ask one question and then ask for an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this stage, it doesn't really matter if they are tendered together or whether they are tendered differently. Perhaps if they are kept different it's even better.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So again, Republika Srpska, Skelani municipality, municipal department of the Ministry of Defence, date 14 November 1992, payment of September salaries. And then in the Bosnian, anyway, it's clear, Fakovici, Radijevici. I think there's a typo in English. It says Rodijevici. Witness, could you read, please, what villages are mentioned there. Payment of September salaries for which villages?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's not waste time on it. It's obvious that it is Radijevici. I don't think that the Prosecution is contesting that. So let's go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So simply this question: September, what year do you think that -- sorry, of what year would that be?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: An exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which also consists of just two pages, one in B/C/S, the other one in English, bearing ERN 04359974, is being tendered and received and marked as Defence Exhibit D836. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. We have another new exhibit. The ERN is 04359970. For the record, in the meantime, I'll read: "14 November 1992, request for finance to be paid to account Skelani SO, Municipal Assembly, payment of salary for August to the Fakovici unit, 546.000 dinars, paid out in cheques."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see that, Mr. Alic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, again, this is dated 14 November 1992, referring to payment for August. Now, you told us yesterday how the Serb soldiers who patrolled around Jagodnja and Joseva and who shot into the village were not, in your opinion, village guards, that their weapons were not those of village guards. This document refers, does it not, to a Fakovici unit? Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it's from the account Skelani Municipal Assembly. That's fine. I don't need your confirmation. I'll just put this question: As regards units in Fakovici, or a unit in Fakovici, on the basis of what you and other people in Jagodnja and Joseva saw in the summer of 1992, what's your estimate of the numbers of Serb soldiers who were based in Fakovici in that period?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, between 200 and 300 people from the accounts of the people who were observing from certain positions that I pointed out Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. on the map yesterday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And I'll just ask for an exhibit number for this document, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This document, Mr. Jones, which contains -- consists of two pages, one in the original B/C/S language and the other one -- and partly handwritten, the other one being the corresponding translation thereof, and which carry ERN 04359970 is being tendered, marked -- and marked as Defence Exhibit D837.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think I just have one more document in this series, which is 04359969, again very similar document to the last one, dated 14 November 1992, request for finance to be paid to account Skelani SO, Municipal Assembly, payment of salary for August to the Fakovici unit, paid out in cash.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does this document confirm, or not, that the Fakovici unit was paid its salary in cash on 14th November 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already pointed out, the Skelani municipality covered the entire area by paying all these soldiers in Fakovici and Radijevici their salaries. That's as far as Skelani municipality is concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll just ask for an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because we have a small problem here. It is -- no it's different. This is a different document. This belongs to the previous one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The difference is cheque and cash.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is where it is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: But it's the same amount paid for the same person?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The amount is illegible on 9969. Our submission is that it's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: It's exactly the same we are dealing with here.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Will Your Honour give me a moment? It could -- Your Honour is quite correct. It could well be the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BRYDENSHOLT
utterances.text: It's the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is probable or it is indicative that we're talking of the same amount probably and the same date, for sure, but definitely in the third handwritten line, that is, the words in brackets -- to me, at least the first two words are identical, but the last word is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the only difference that I see, and of course the amount, both in figures and in words, in the new documents that you are seeking to tender, is pretty much illegible, but it is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Not only that, Your Honour. I think it's probably right also to say that if one looks closely where it says "dinars," that it looks -- the way the numbers are on the lines that it is -- in fact that bit is identical. I think the carbon copy -- the invention of the carbon copy might explain how we can have two copies which are identical in some respects but with different writing in other parts of it. I wouldn't want to venture too much into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I don't think this is going to be a problem. Do you seek to tender this document into evidence, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document, which consists of two pages, ERN 04359969, two pages, as I said, one in B/C/S, partly in handwritten format, and the other one being the corresponding translation into English thereof, is being tendered, received, and marked as Defence Exhibit D838.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm moving to a different area altogether now, so we'll leave exhibits for a little while.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the period after events in Fakovici on the 5th of October, 1992, until the end of the year. And if you could just describe for us what the situation was like in your villages after Fakovici and toward the end of 1992, just briefly, that would help set the scene.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation was exceptionally difficult. Upon my return from Zanjevo and when I entered the village of Jagodnja, I arrived at about 1.00 a.m. and my parents believed that I had been killed. Therefore, the situation was difficult at the time. In addition, there was the daily shelling of our villages, with the units coming in from all sides, frequent incursions, people being wounded. And other people fleeing from parts of Joseva for fear of being caught and slain. And there were people coming over from other villages in search of food. All in all, we had a large number of refugees in the village who would go to Fakovici and Abdulici on a daily basis to look for food. Many people were killed. We ourselves had no idea where all of those people were from. Nobody went out to vacate the bodies; that would have been impossible. So, for example, in Abdulici, in Zanjevo, people would go to the field to pick the corn that was already overripe. It was too late to harvest. But the field, the cornfield was mined, so many people were killed there. Lots of people went there and went back.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You've told us how -- about the difficulties of getting the bodies of people who had been killed. On the 5th of October, 1992, you mentioned how four people were killed in land-mines. Were you able to retrieve those bodies?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those four people who were killed, two of them on the 5th of October, their bodies were retrieved immediately. Two days later, a man came along from Osad [phoen], I believe. This is a place near Kragljivoda. He was crying and he told us that his brother had been killed in the area. He asked us to please give him a hand to try and retrieve the body. So we decided to set out - and I was part of that group - go all the way behind Radijevici, a village that had not yet fallen. The soldiers had not yet entered the village. We knew that there were those two bodies there that had been left behind, and eventually we reached this area. It was very difficult to access the area. There was a large open area and the forest right there. Once we got to the bodies, we had already learned that Serb soldiers sometimes booby-trapped dead bodies. We brought a length of rope along and a stretcher, we would use just two sticks and put a blanket between them. Once we got to the bodies, we tied them up, both bodies. They were nearby. One of the booby-traps went off underneath one of the bodies. The bodies were torn to shreds by the explosion. The weather was warm, so the bodies had already begun to rot, and the hair had already begun to fall off; therefore, it was a very difficult situation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in short, the Serbs had actually booby-trapped these dead bodies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any idea why they would do that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I do. The people who did that, who booby-trapped the bodies in order to get someone else killed, they used the opportunity to set other booby-traps, because they knew that sooner or later someone would come to try to pull the bodies out. And the aim was to kill other people as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you've mentioned in your testimony already how you had lookouts from Jagodnja and Joseva. Among other things, you've mentioned that they saw, did they see movement of boats across the Drina?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask if the witness could be shown D43, please. And for the record, this is concerning Zarko Bozic, born in Bratunac, who was a soldier of the 3rd Infantry Battalion. And it says: "Bozic Zarko has been in the RS army since the beginning of war activities. He took part in combats in the area of Fakovici and Skelani." And then leaving the part about his positive character attributes, it says at the end: "The above-mentioned person drowned in the Drina on January 9, 1993, transporting MTS and food from storage in FRY for the needs of his unit."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, this refers to the transportation of MTS in January 1993 and food. Firstly, actually, do you know what MTS refers to?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: MTS could be ammunition or weapons or even medicines, that sort of thing. That's my opinion, at least. MTS usually refers to medication, equipment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And this refers to that being done, or at least the person drowning in January 1993, transporting that material. Are you aware of whether that material was transported in this way in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, is he talking about being transported by this person in relationship to this document or just transports of types of material like that in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. I'll deal with that. May I raise one issue, Your Honour. I understood the practice was that counsel stands up and then waits for an indication from Your Honour as to whether or not to speak. I've noticed that that hasn't been observed over the last couple of days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, not really. It depends. One usually uses his discretion and judgement in anticipation of what -- most of the time, as you know, we anticipate what is going to be objected and most of the time, sort of, it's reading the mind of counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We've been rebuked quite strongly I should say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On occasions, yes. And on occasions, as you know, I've stopped the Prosecution and they wait. But this is the kind of objection that I wasn't -- or seeking clarification that I had in mind to. So that's why I allow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We just ask for equal treatment, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. Many a time you are allowed to do this exactly the same. You are allowed while the previous cross-examination was taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question -- I may have to stop the transcript now to find what it was. I'll put it more broadly. Firstly, are you aware of any material being transported from Serbia into Fakovici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what our observers told us who were in these places that I marked on the map. They observed boats crossing from Serbia into Bosnia, and then the same boats would go back across the Drina near Radijevica Potok, as well as between Fakovici and Bacevci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know what was being transported? Were you able, you or these lookouts, to observe what was being transported?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Our observers used binoculars to monitor this activity. It's the sort of the binoculars that hunters use. There were men on those boats and crates, or parcels. That, at least, was what they told us when they came back from observing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what time period was this?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after people had left Zanjevo. Those people, too, followed the boats, but there was no information on what the boats were carrying. They just told us that the boats were moving in that direction. So that was after the attack, in July, or rather, early June. It was on a daily basis that our observers moved around the area. Sometimes they would go further down, whenever it was possible, when there were no Serb patrols around, they would travel through the woods in order to obtain just this kind of information, whether an attack was perhaps imminent, whether shelling was imminent, or not, throughout this period of time. This was a huge forest where you could move about and still avoid the Serb patrols.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, moving to a new area. Do you know a place called Glogova?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some stage before -- well, I won't fix a time period. At some stage did someone come to your village and tell you what was happening in Glogova?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Early in 1993, it might have been January, the 1st, the 2nd, the 3rd, the 4th - I don't know - early January, all in all, a man arrived. I wasn't there myself; I was with the wounded. He came and he asked to see Asim Smajlovic. So they met, they talked, and he requested help in order to move on to Glogova, because they were facing a difficult situation. There was no food for them and Serbs from attacking from Kravica [Realtime transcript read in error "Kragljivoda"] and from Bratunac, from both directions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to this person personally?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at this point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he had come from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he said he had come from Goluba [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know if anyone sent him?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that Ejub Golic had sent him. The first time I ever heard of that person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones, because I see that line 8, he -- at least the answer -- the transcript says he came from "Goluba." And I think it's important that we establish that he meant or he said Glogova and --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I was about to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: There's another thing as well in the transcript which is page 23, line 4, or 3, "Kragljivoda and from Bratunac" and I think we all heard Kravica and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, going back to this: When I said where this man came from, I meant what area. What village did he come from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Glogova; that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned Ejub Golic. Had you heard of him before this time?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, he was asking for help in Glogova. Did any of you from Jagodnja and Joseva go to help?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Asim Smajlovic asked people to volunteer to go there and to help those people. Immediately, between 10 and 15 people volunteered and he then asked me whether I was willing to join those people, as I was the only nurse around. I'm not sure how I should put it. Therefore, I decided to join these fighters who had suffered so much at Jagodnja. I was afraid that the same thing might befall them again, namely, they would be injured and there would be no one to dress their wounds. So that was the reason why I decided to join.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. I think when you said "I'm not sure how I should put it," you weren't sure whether to say medical sister or medical brother. That was the terminological confusion.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that would be one way of putting it. Probably not really medical sister; perhaps brother, medical brother.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Did Asim Smajlovic go along? Was he in this group of 10 to 15 people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I don't know if you can show us on the map, if you're provided with the map again, the route. If you could trace the route you took.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Obviously it may be difficult for you to be precise, but if you can just indicate without drawing exactly with the pointer where you went.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I won't draw. So there is Jagodnja, the way out of Jagodnja, and there is an area where there's just a forest and we were going to Kravica through this forest all the way to Murselovici, and below Osmace, and we got down to Zeleni Jadar, which stretches across this area. So this is Jadar and then we went this way through Jadar and we got out just above Pusmulici, and then we went down to the village of Bajramovici. It is not indicated on the map because -- yeah, it just isn't on the map. So it should be somewhere here, the village called Bajramovici. You can't see it on this map, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We may have another map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But for my purposes, I simply wanted to ask you this: Is it right, then, that you didn't go through Srebrenica on your way to Glogova?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there any reason why you didn't go through Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This man who was our guide, who was with us in this group, who had come from Glogova, he -- through Srebrenica and he said that there were shellings all the time and that at that time we should have gone below Srebrenica, in the direction of Potocari, where there were snipers from an area called Zvijezda, I believe, and therefore it is not possible to go through the corridor with a group of about 15 people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. How long did it take you to get to the Glogova area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately two days, travelling on foot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where -- if you know, where exactly did you arrive after those two days? What village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that the name of the village was Cizmici. It is near Bljeceva. Before the war, I had never been there, and it was the first time I was there on that occasion. We got there at dusk, and we were told the name of the village was Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what did you do that evening, and what did you do the next day?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That evening when we got there, when we got to Cizmici, we entered a house and some people welcomed us. I don't know who they were. And we had dinner. We had our own food in our backpacks. And I was a bit tired, so I took a nap. And at some point after midnight, maybe 2 or 3.00 a.m., somebody came along and said that we had to get up and go and move towards Glogova, I suppose. And we were given some white ribbons that we tied across our foreheads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know roughly what date this was?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the night between the 6th and the 7th of January.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So then did you set off and go towards Glogova on the 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We went from there. There were quite a few civilians there, people walking around the village. It was total chaos and it was all in dark, during the night, and we went and followed this man who was walking in front of us. And he led us through the woods and creeks, and there was snow on the ground, and it was so difficult that it was almost impossible to stand all that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say there were quite a few civilians there. Can you give us an idea of the numbers of civilians that you saw in the area that morning?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that morning, or during the night, and at daybreak -- I mean, it wasn't really possible to count, but there were thousands of civilians with backpacks and there was a total confusion. And they were walking in front of us, behind us, and we couldn't really make out where our own group members were in that confusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned how you were given some white ribbons that you tied across your foreheads. You've mentioned these civilians. Did any of these civilians wear white ribbons as well, or was it only your group?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some civilians had that as well, and everybody I could see. It was -- quite simply, I can't explain to you what it looked like.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So you say: "Some civilians had that as well, and everybody I could see." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, the civilians were wearing those white ribbons across their foreheads.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were all of them wearing white ribbons, thousands of them, or only some of them?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I can't tell you about thousands of people, but the group that I saw, the people that were around me, we all had those white ribbons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Okay. I think that's clear. Now, during the day, was there any shelling at any stage?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the course of that morning, as we were approaching - I was told we were going towards Glogova and that we were approaching Glogova - shooting and shelling started. I don't know where exactly it came from. But when we approached the village, at that moment, I was told that the name of the village was Jezestica. That's my recollection. And we were in that forest. A great deal of shooting came out of that village behind those houses, and I realised that it wasn't Glogova, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to take this bit by bit now. This village which you were told was Jezestica, was it on a hill or in a valley?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were in the forest. And as soon as we came out of the forest, there were houses not far away, maybe a hundred or 200 metres away, maybe a little bit further. I can't tell you exactly, because this was a long time ago. And then there was a kind of valley behind those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the houses, were they in the valley or were they on the hill?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you. They were halfway up, next to the forest. I really can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say "a great deal of shooting came out of that village, Jezestica," as you've described, "behind those houses." Was the shooting coming from behind the house or --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Let me just finish my question. Was the shooting coming from the houses or from some other location behind the houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting came mostly from where I was, from those houses, and higher up, where other people were. I think there was a four-barrelled weapon, and I was told that it was being used all the time incessantly and there was shooting coming from those houses all the time. Basically, there was shooting coming out of every single house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you. Now, you mentioned these civilians who were in the area. In your opinion, or to your knowledge, was it possible to prevent these civilians from going into this area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why do you say that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because, and I've already mentioned this, I mentioned this yesterday in my statement, people were following even the smallest group of people who were armed, they went in the direction of shelling, shooting, where the action was, any kind of action. Because they were expecting to find food, clothes, or anything else that might be useful for sheer survival.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the shooting from these houses that you've described, were these Serbs or Muslims shooting from the houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Serbs who were shooting from those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did they manage to resist or did the village fall?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put up resistance, but within a short period of time, the village did in fact fall. Actually, the civilians entered the village even before the army, before the armed groups, I mean, and people who had arms, they went in before. And when we entered, when I myself entered the village, I came across a bakery, and it was full of bread, and the bread was fresh, and I couldn't wait to get my hands on a loaf of bread, to eat some bread, because this type of bread, white bread, was something that I hadn't even set my eyes on for about six months. So people were actually elbowing one another out of the way, trying to get their hands on the food and make sure that they can get some food and take it back to Srebrenica or back to the villages that they had come from. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So you said the civilians entered the village even before the men who were bearing arms; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've described how they were essentially fighting for food, elbowing each other out of the way. Did you see -- let me put it this way: As far as you know, did the civilians have any interest in burning houses in that village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look, those civilians who came there, setting houses on fire was the least of their worries. Whoever got there, got there only and exclusively to find food, clothes, footwear, and I see no reason whatsoever why any civilian would have wanted to set any houses on fire at that time, before entering, because I myself went into two houses and I found first aid kits, medicines, bandages and I collected all that. I mean, some people wouldn't even look at that. It was not their top priority. Their priority was food and clothes. And at that stage, I didn't see a single house in Jezestica being set on fire. There were people who were injured, and I tried to dress their wounds and give them first aid, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people were injured, roughly?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About ten people that I myself attended to at that stage, and I offered first aid to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what had they been wounded by? Was it from shooting or from shelling or from both?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: People were injured by both bullets and shells, and shells were landing from the direction of Kravica, as was mentioned before. And I was in a position which I didn't know where Kravica was or where Glogova was. But the other people who were there, they were more familiar with the area and they told me that the shells were coming from Kravica, from the direction of Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think the -- that will be corrected later, Kravica, yes, in line 24.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've mentioned how you went into a bakery. Did you take food away from there or did you eat it straight away?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ate a warm loaf of bread on the spot; it was good.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter unfortunately didn't hear the last sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you hear that, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry. Could you repeat your answer, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. You asked me whether I ate the bread on the spot or whether I put it in my backpack; and I replied that I ate it on the spot, and I can still remember how good it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was that before the shelling or shooting, or that was in the midst of shelling or shooting that you ate this bread?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the midst of shelling and shooting, because those were the first houses that we entered. The first house was the bakery, which was on the border of the woods, and it was easy to get into that house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at what time of day was it now? You said how you set off in the morning. What time of day was it, let's say, when you went into the bakery?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit difficult. Roughly speaking, between 8.00 and 9.00. I can't tell you exactly. Because what sticks in your mind is -- well, at least as far as I'm concerned, my recollection of Kravica has to do with this bread that I ate there. I can't tell you what time it was. At any point between 7.00 a.m. and 9.00 a.m., according to my estimation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it still dark at that stage or was it light?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't dark, of course. It was already light.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did you stay in Jezestica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself stayed at Jezestica for a very short time. There were some injured, and these people from my group decided that I should go in the direction -- well, basically we went down to the asphalt road. I don't know what the name of the area was. And we came out to a place called Avdagina Njive, if I remember correctly, and then we moved towards Cizmici together with the injured. I myself was going together with the injured. And I'm not really personally familiar with what happened afterwards in Kravica, around Kravica, and Glogova. So I myself accompanied the injured to Cizmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And finally, just on Jezestica, how would you describe the shelling which you experienced in Jezestica? Was it light shelling, medium shelling, heavy shelling?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view -- well, I mean, every shell is heavy. So a single shell, even a single shell, is a serious matter, because it can kill people. So there was a lot of shelling from the direction of Kravica. I can't tell you exactly how many shells landed there, but basically there were shells coming from that direction. And as far as I can tell, the destruction caused was extremely serious. Even if a single man is killed, it's serious shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you return to Jagodnja and Joseva after this?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did the return journey take you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, about two days, because we were tired, exhausted. And we tended to rest a little bit longer. And I was waiting for those people from my group who had stayed behind. I waited for them at Cizmici, and then we continued on our journey. Some of them were carrying food, some were carrying clothes or cigarettes that they found. And so we were fully loaded, as we used to say. We had a full load of food and I myself had found some medicines, et cetera. And so we continued on our way to Jagodnja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did there come a time when Jagodnja fell to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Jagodnja?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb presence in Jagodnja -- or rather, look, I think you should clarify this yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies. I think it must have been the interpretation, because I --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a time in 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the date, if you know?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jagodnja fell, in my view -- actually, the attacks lasted -- could I just try and clarify this, as when the attacks at Jagodnja started?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... this, Mr. Jones?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because if he wants to clarify, I will let him clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like him to, and I'd like to just say something to clarify it even more, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So go ahead, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: May I precede that, Your Honour? I'd like to make an explanation first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My apologies, Mr. Alic, I skipped, obviously, from January 1993 to a time considerably later, and I should have let you know that I was going to move to a later period. So my apologies. I think that was the problem. I wanted to start with when Jagodnja and Joseva fell completely to the Serbs, and then work back from there. So if you can just tell me when Jagodnja and Joseva fell to the Serbs, then we'll proceed from there.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attacks that followed in March 1993 started on around the 5th, the 6th, the 7th, up until the day when the village fell. As to shelling, well, there was daily shelling from Serbia, from multi-barrelled mortars, from the direction of Fakovici, mortars were being used at Fakovici and Bijeli Kamen, and those were horrendous days, probably the worst days of my life, after starvation, after suffering the cold throughout the winter, there was this powerful attack, relentless attacks day and night, and sometimes a single weapon would fire 16 shells in one go. And they were aiming at the village of Hasanovici, which had not been set on fire. There were about 10, a dozen houses there, and sometimes shells would set fire to stables or sometimes those stables or houses were set on fire. We had some houses with wooden tiles or thatched roofs, and so those were bloody days that one can't forget very easily. And also there was an area including the road out of the village and we could no longer move there, and we were fully surrounded as of the 10th of March by the JNA. And we found that those were only and exclusively the soldiers from the JNA, and they were armed to their teeth, basically. And we fell on the 12th or the 13th of March, 1993, because we just had to move out. We had to run away. We were fully surrounded. And the group of people who had some weapons tried to push their way in the direction of Biljeg, through a forest, during the night. And it was a rocky area. There were craggy rocks there. And when we crossed over to Biljeg, we were ambushed by the Serb forces. And about ten people were wounded on that occasion. And when we crossed over to the village, Miholjevine, I saw that my father and mother were missing and quite a few other family it members. And therefore, on the very same evening we had to go back to Jagodnja, and there was a forest above Jagodnja where those people were hiding. There were about 100 people, elderly people, women, children, who were not able to get out at that stage. So we tried once again to cross over together with them and we had other injured and wounded by the Serb soldiers, and my father and three women were captured on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. That's very helpful, that detail. I need to go back for one or two matters. You say the attacks that followed in March started on the 5th, 6th, and 7th. What month is that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And before March, between January and March, was it peaceful in Jagodnja and Joseva or were there also attacks and shelling?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the arrival, or rather, after the first half of January 1993, there was the very same shelling from Serbia, from those areas, and between the 20th of January and the 30th of January, there was shelling on a daily basis, as well as infantry attacks. And our villages, I mean, Joseva, for example, was completely surrounded. And in that month of January we suffered huge losses in terms of the people killed. Many people were killed, civilians, and they set fire to stables and about 30 animals in those stables, cattle. And our cattle was in the stables, and everything was set on fire; and it was just horrible. And believe me, it is very difficult for me to talk about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll be moving on. But in other words, then, there were attacks and shelling and all the terrible things you've described in January as well, January and February, but only in the beginning of March did the final offensive take place; is that a fair summary?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as I said in my first statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've described now in the attack in March, the use of artillery, and you said that one weapon could shoot 16 shells in one go. Do you know what that's referred to, that particular weapon?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a multi-barrelled rocket launcher, VBR, as we used to call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And can you explain to the Trial Chamber the sort of damage that a VBR can do to houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A VBR can raze your house down to the ground. It can set it on fire; a shell can set a house on fire. I tried to explain this a couple of minutes ago. So if you have a stable which is full of hay, and all this is flammable, and of course it would be set on fire by shells, VBRs, any kind of shell at that time can land on a roof of a house. Because we were watching all that, and it was really and truly horrible. And it was almost impossible to follow everything. And we would go down a road, and one shell would be landing across the road, in front of us, the other behind us, within a perimeter of ten metres you would have several shells landing at any given time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you mentioned Hasanovici, a hamlet of Jagodnja. Can you explain what damage was caused to Hasanovici by shells.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In March 1993, on the 13th or the 12th, Hasanovici fell. It remained under the control of the Serbs and we moved out. In January 1993, likewise, Hasanovici had been destroyed, devastated. Some houses were torched at that time as a result of shelling. Therefore, from January to March we were still at Jagodnja and Joseva, staying in whatever houses were still there and were habitable. People would mend some of the damage, things that had burned down, but we stayed until as late as March. After March, however, it was impossible to survive in the area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Hasanovici was devastated by shelling; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I have a -- with the usher's assistance, a new exhibit for the witness. It's ERN 04284977. Uzice Corps command, strictly confidential number 173-13, dated January 27, 1993. And it's addressed to VRS RS army, Drina Corps command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In this regard, in fact, there's also, I think, a correction for the transcript, or perhaps of interpretation. You referred to the Yugoslav army being involved in 1993. Is that correct, Yugoslav army rather than the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav army, the Yugoslav army, the Yugoslav People's Army. I'm no longer sure myself what they call it. Those were people from Serbia, active-service Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's very clear. Thank you. Looking at this document, first of all, Uzice Corps command, do you know what Uzice is?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never been to Uzice myself, but I know that it is in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to this, the command of that corps in Serbia, on the 27th of January, 1993, was addressing the VRS, RS army Drina Corps command, i.e., a command in Serbia addressing the Republika Srpska army. Is that correct? Do you see the reference to VRS there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to read -- that's fine. I'm going to read a section of this document. I'm going to start below the three numbered paragraphs: "In our combat activities so far, we inflicted huge losses to the enemy in the village of Mlecevo, Jagodnja, Joseva, the village of Daljegosta, Arapovici, the village of Pavkovici, the village of Tihici, the village of Milicevici, Osmace, the village of Tokoljac, and Jezero." Now, firstly, you see the mention of huge losses inflicted on Jagodnja and Joseva. Can you confirm that that was the case prior to 27 January 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look at the other villages which I've just read out. Mlecevo. Now, was that before the war a Serb or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So is it correct that this is apparently a call from Serbia informing the VRS that huge losses had been inflicted on the enemy in a Serb village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that, sir?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. According to this document, huge losses were inflicted to the enemy in the village of Mlecevo; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't in Mlecevo to know what the losses there were. I was at Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just referring to what's in this document. Let me put a different question. You've told us that Mlecevo was a Serb village before the war. In your experience, in this time, Serb artillery --

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in your experience, in this period, did Serb artillery sometimes fire indiscriminately on Serb and Muslim villages alike when they were retaking an area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, certainly. Yes. Yes. They targeted everyone alike. They made no distinction between Serb and Muslim villages. They used this multiple rocket launcher to fire on all these areas, also the other areas, Godzevici, Prijnos [phoen], Daljegosta, all the other villages too. They were cleansing the area indiscriminately. I'm not sure how to explain this. It was a single line that was moving, clearing the area, all the way to Srebrenica, irregardless of who was where. Because these soldiers had no idea where Muslims were and where Serbs were. They had been given a map and they just targeted everyone alike.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Arapovici, was that a Serb or Muslim village before the war?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arapovici was a Serb village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Jezero, was that in Serb hands in 1992 and early 1993?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm moving to a new area, so I'm finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd just ask for an exhibit number, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This document which consists in one page in B/C/S language and two pages in the corresponding translation thereof into English is being received and marked as Defence Exhibit D839. The ERN number is 04284977.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to ask you some questions going back to 1992 just about Asim Smajlovic and the people in Jagodnja and Joseva. So just so you know we're moving to a new area. You've told us how you appointed Asim Smajlovic to be your leader in Jagodnja and Joseva in 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he answer to any other leader, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware if orders were ever received in Jagodnja and Joseva in 1992 from outside?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, did Asim Smajlovic in 1992 go to Srebrenica to attend meetings?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you -- well, explain why you say that. Are you in a position to say whether he did or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And explain why you -- how you know that.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because he was in Jagodnja and Joseva throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, dealing with the fighters in Jagodnja and Joseva, did they have uniforms in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have ranks, like captain, lieutenant, colonel?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have a barracks?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have an armoury?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they receive salaries for fighting?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that time, 1992, was there any way of making someone do something which he didn't want to do, for example, to go to fight when he preferred to stay at home?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. There was no way that anyone could force anyone else or tell them to go somewhere, that they had to go somewhere and do something about these combat operations, or anything else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think the way it's come out in the transcript, we'll need clarification. That's all one sentence as I heard it. There was no way -- tell me if this is correct. You said there was no way that anyone could force anyone else or tell them to go somewhere. I'm going to have to start again, because the way it's come out is not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- basically, however, I think that the first sentence of his answer explains it all. So if you want to pursue it, do so by all means, but I think it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, for the record, then, I want to make clear that it was: No way that anyone could force anyone or tell them to do -- to go somewhere, no way that anyone could tell them that they had to go somewhere and do something. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, yes. No one could order anyone else to go somewhere they didn't want to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I would actually -- I may subsequently ask for a correction to the transcript to include a comma, because that's not a fair rendition, but Your Honour has confirmed that, so I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was anyone ever punished for desertion or cowardice if they ran away during combat?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, and based on your experience, was there any way of doing that, of punishing someone for desertion or cowardice?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people in fact in Jagodnja and Joseva do as they pleased, essentially?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please clarify that?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think that's fine. I'll withdraw that question and put this question instead: Was there any meaningful way of issuing orders in Jagodnja and Joseva in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving to another area, but I think I can cover it before the break. In 1992 -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Make sure of that, because the witness is getting tired.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: In that case, I think perhaps it's best to pause now and then to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a 30-minute break starting from now. That means we'll start at a quarter to 1.00 or just past it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you. I anticipate I'll conclude in about half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic, in 1992, did you know someone called Ahmo Tihic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before the war, do you know what his activities were?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Ahmo Tihic was a cattle merchant. He was an entrepreneur and he owned a butchery at Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he wealthy or poor?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a wealthy person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he politically active, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know with which political party?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he's from, what village?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Tihici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then that's in what area?
