utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Skelani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he still in his village of Tihici in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why not?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because the Muslims had been expelled from that area in early May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know where he went from Tihici?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he was in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The summer of 1992, in late July, a man arrived in Jagodnja and Joseva, telling us to go to a place called Biljeg. Asim Smajlovic, myself, and another three or four men went across the woods and reached the place eventually. We found Ahmo Tihic at Biljeg, in the woods. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Biljeg -- was it an inhabited or uninhabited area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the forest. There were no buildings there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know why -- or why did you go along with these other men to Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, we didn't even think about the reason. Once we got there, however, something was being said about help being exchanged between Jagodnja and Joseva, on the one hand, and Biljeg, on the other. Ahmo Tihic proposed that we should join forces with him in order to defend these areas. We asked for Ahmo Tihic and his group of people, who were at Biljeg, to go to Jagodnja and Joseva so that we could join forces in defending ourselves from the Serb soldiers there. However, he simply replied, "I can't accept that." He smiled and he said, "There's no need for me to go to Jagodnja and Joseva." The distance must have been seven or eight kilometres across the woods. So no agreement was reached about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just why did you personally go along with this group to Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this time, it wasn't safe to go to Biljeg, so Asim told me -- asked me if I'd like to join them. I had my bag with the first-aid kit and I set out. There was a risk that if we were ambushed on the way, somebody would be injured, so I was there to give assistance to whoever had been wounded or injured.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that in fact this proposal for the help between Biljeg and Jagodnja and Joseva didn't come to anything; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know someone called Almas Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where he's from?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almas Hasanovic is from Zanjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your conversations with Ahmo Tihic, either then or later, did he ever say anything about Almas Hasanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early August, we found out, because a man had arrived from Biljeg -- actually, several people. It was never one man alone moving in that direction, because it was an enormous forest, there could have been Serbs controlling the area or anyone else who happened to be there. Two or three persons arrived - I can't remember exactly - they met Asim Smajlovic and told him to go to Biljeg. He went, and I was there myself, along with these several other people. We came to Biljeg. We found Ahmo in the woods there. There were some makeshift chairs made of wood. Almas Hasanovic was seated next to Ahmo Tihic. Ahmo told us that someone from Srebrenica had sent Almas Hasanovic from Zanjevo to take over this group of people at Biljeg. He just smiled and he said that nobody could lead that group of people at Biljeg. He proposed to Asim, here's this man, and he can take the group to Jagodnja and Joseva, in order for him to more easily reach his village of Joseva [as interpreted]. On our way back to Jagodnja, Asim Smajlovic told me personally, "Since Ahmo Tihic doesn't want me, I don't want him either."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Just going back to that, Ahmo Tihic smiled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Jones. Yes, Ms. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness said, On our way back he told me personally if Ahmo Tihic doesn't want him, therefore Almas, I don't want him either. And what I see recorded here, If Tihic doesn't want me, I don't want him either, which is a totally different meaning, if you think about what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. If you could just tell us what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones. Perhaps you could take this ...

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you tell us what Asim Smajlovic said about -- about Almas Hasanovic.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Asim Smajlovic said what I said. He said, "If Ahmo Tihic does not want to accept Almas Hasanovic at Biljeg, then I will not accept him as the leader of the group at Jagodnja and Joseva either."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And also I think we need to correct the transcript where it says "Ahmo proposed Asim, Here's this man and he can take the group to Jagodnja and Joseva in order for him to more easily reach his village of ..." And what village was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zanjevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Jones, for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as far as the proposal from someone from Srebrenica, there was -- you told us that Almas Hasanovic should take over the group of people at Biljeg. Who at that time was in fact, to your knowledge, heading the group at Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The group at Biljeg was headed by Ahmo Tihic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So in other words, someone from Srebrenica sent Almas Hasanovic to take over from Ahmo, and Ahmo Tihic smiled at that idea and didn't accept it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did Almas stay in the Jagodnja and Joseva area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almas Hasanovic had no weapon or anything. He was a fine young man, my generation. We were personal acquaintances. He spent about 15 days in Jagodnja. He lingered about the area. We still had food. And after those 15 days, he left for Biljeg. I have no idea where he ended up after that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you know about the background of Almas Hasanovic in terms of his education or military training?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Almas Hasanovic was a military official. He had completed a military academy before the war. That's one thing I know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to Biljeg and you heard that he was being proposed to head a group, how did you feel about that? Did you have any feelings one way or the other?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We thought it would turn out like that, that Almas Hasanovic, being a military official, would take over command of the group at Biljeg. We were pleased and there was a palpable relief among us. However, when it turned out that this would not be the case, we were disappointed and not feeling very pleasant, in general.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, perhaps for one -- may I interrupt you for a minute. Mr. Alic, could you indicate on the map where Biljeg is, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. Right here, in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Perhaps you could mark that with a pen, with a "B."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And for the record, the witness marks with a "B" the site where he maintains Biljeg is, and this is in the proximity of Miholjevine, beneath the range of mountains that is called Orlova Bukva [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Asim Smajlovic also didn't accept the idea of Almas Hasanovic being any type of leader in Jagodnja and Joseva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, knowing the people of this -- of your area and the times, can you help us with this: Was it possible for people to come from outside a village to come in and take over command? Was that something which happened or which could happen?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That wasn't possible. No one trusted anyone else by this time. There was no chance of anyone coming from anywhere else to take over command or issue orders or lead that group of people in our village, or any other village, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is that the explanation for why Almas Hasanovic was neither the leader in Biljeg or in Jagodnja and Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd like to show a video, that's P433, and we're starting at 5400, and then going to around 5810. So it's about four minutes. There's a transcript, P433.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I just want to pause for a second to see if --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, can you hear the words which are being spoken? I know it's faint, but are you able to hear?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Okay. We can play it, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there is a whole lot of background noise, and it's annoying. I can't listen properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I very much doubt if we can find a solution to that. We are hearing the same as you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. It's the quality of the video.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's why, Mr. Alic, if you can just bear with the background noise, if you are able to hear what's being said. It's a four-minute section and then I'll have questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not going to last long. I mean, please explain that to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's brief.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to ask you there, first of all, do you recognise the man who's being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ahmo Tihic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you recognise the area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the forest at Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you know the other gentleman who is doing the interview. Do you?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you will have heard -- or let me put it this way: Did you hear it being said that Ahmo Tihic went up to that area to defend the terrain in Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I'll read what we have in our transcript and see if it corresponds to what you did hear: "A man called Tihic says: "In Skelani, when the Serbian extremists seized the police station, we retreated with these armed men. We went up there to Kragljivoda. For the most part, people did not want to accept us anywhere. People were avoiding us. They were afraid of torching. Wherever we went, whatever village we came to, they sent us away. Most of the combatants who were with me are together with me now." My question is just this: Did you understand that to be the situation of Ahmo Tihic and his men, that they weren't actually able to settle in a village and had to settle in this uninhabited area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't know if you're familiar with Robin Hood in your country. Is that someone -- a character you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it a similar situation that we're describing here, a man and his band of men in the woods?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we see that Ahmo Tihic is in some kind of uniform, although it's not so clear from his footwear, but the others are just in ordinary clothes. Is that how they appeared in the video, is that how they appeared when you saw them in the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I saw those people, I mean, Ahmo Tihic had no uniform at all, and these other people were also wearing civilian clothes, T-shirts, pants, and they had rather primitive and shoddy footwear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll continue playing the video, and please listen as carefully as you can to what's being said.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. We can stop that there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear Fakovici mentioned in that video?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you heard the -- Ahmo Tihic saying, "They are still shelling with the heavy weaponry, with the artillery. They are shelling from Fakovici down there under Zljebac."

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the date on the screen appears to be 14th of August, 1992. We can't see it so clearly now, but we saw it in another frame. Does that fit in with your experience of the situation in Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, do we have a date when he himself went to Biljeg? He may have said it and I may not recall it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: He mentioned once in end of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. I just wanted to establish whether it is a time proximate to what we are seeing on the screen now or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I think there are two visits he referred to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you remind us, please, Mr. Alic, when the two trips to Biljeg took place.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was there twice, by the end of July and between the beginning and mid-August. I can't remember the exact date, but the first half of August.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And we briefly saw a sort of structure there, a canvas, a sort of tent-like structure. When you went to Biljeg, did you see any solid buildings?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There are no facilities of any sort of around Biljeg. I could perhaps illustrate it on a map, but at any rate, there are no houses, no buildings, no outbuildings, stables, nothing of the sort.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit. I'll ask if the witness could please be shown Prosecution Exhibit 80, P80, and P94. I may as well have that be shown at the same time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just for the record, since this is a lengthy document, we reviewed this document, did we not, in our offices when you came here to The Hague?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just for the record, it's Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Srebrenica armed forces staff, the date is 19 September 1993, breakdown of the formation structure of Srebrenica OS during the past period. Now, we have first formation structure on 20 May 1992, Srebrenica TO staff was formed in Bajramovici; from 17 April 1992 to mid-October 1992 the first regional units were formed under the auspices of the TO, namely -- and I won't force you to go through all of this. But I can certainly state for the record that Jagodnja and Joseva is not mentioned anywhere there. Would you agree that even on -- in October 1992, no armed group from Jagodnja and Joseva was even on paper within the structure of the -- of any Srebrenica TO staff?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think this --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him answer this question first and then we see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We were not in any of these TO structures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sellers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my question -- or my objection was more specific in terms of not being able to say that any -- that not -- that Jagodnja and Joseva was not even on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But the question was in relation to what is shown on this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: I don't know whether that was in relationship to the document, because I believe that Defence counsel has said that that is not in the document, and this document dates from 1993, according to what's clearly on its face. And I believe the question went to October 1992, in paperwork of October 1992, which isn't before Mr. Alic at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. But he said even in October of 1992, that was what Mr. Jones asked or pointed out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, Mr. Jones, what's your reaction to this? Because I think I understood perfectly well what your question was.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Well, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That basically, as I understood you, you were stating or putting to the witness that even as far as October 1992, there was no such thing as a TO Jagodnja and the other one.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if you look at the document, it wasn't -- it didn't even show up on the document itself. That's how I understood your question to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. And I'm happy with the answer which was given by the witness, so if that's allowed to stand, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: It would be very long for me to have him first confirm that for the first three pages there's no mention of Jagodnja and Joseva; we can see that for ourselves. And he's confirmed that substantively, up to October 1992, they were not in any TO unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we go to page 3 in English, the second formation structure, this is dealing with the situation from 14 October 1992. See the operation staff -- and my apologies. It's the next page. "On 14 October 1992, following the commander's order, the units were again reorganised as follows," and then we have a list of these various units. And I want to go to page 6 in the English, and it's point 6 in B/C/S, page 4 in B/C/S. It says: "Number 6: Independent Biljeg Battalion, based in Biljeg, commander, Ahmo Tihic." Have you found that part?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, if we look there, it says: "3rd Company, based in Joseva, commander, Mefail Ridzic." Do you know Mefail Ridzic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did he come to Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly when Mefail came there. Probably in November 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how long did he remain in the area?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He stayed there until the fall of Jagodnja and Joseva. He was there. He was coming and going, and a couple of other people from the village of Zanjevo. He was also from Zanjevo. So they were just coming and going. And there was this movement of people in that area where he himself was killed, together with two people in -- between Jagodnja and Joseva. I think it was on the 10th of March. I'm not really sure that it was the 10th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say a couple of other people from the village of Zanjevo. Was he -- oh, yes, you've said he was from Zanjevo. So he was coming -- going between Zanjevo and Jagodnja and Joseva; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Between Jagodnja and Biljeg. So these people went towards Zanjevo as well to collect food. I think they had links to that area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, between November 1992 and March 1993, was he any type of commander in Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the fighters in Joseva ever under any sort of command or orders of Mefail Ridzic?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there, right up until the fall of Joseva, any military formation, like a company, a military-formed unit?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was just a group of armed men who were defending their village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was there at the same period any military-formed unit in Biljeg, namely, a battalion, as claimed in this document?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never heard of the battalion, but I heard about a group of people that was at Biljeg.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And up until the fall of Joseva, was Joseva under the command of Biljeg?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not under anybody's command. We acted independently and we were defending ourselves independently and did whatever we had to do in that way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, after Jagodnja and Joseva fell to the Serbs, did those places remain in Serb hands?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be right that in April 1993, it would have been impossible for Muslim units to be based in Joseva, because that was actually held by the Serbs at that date?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. After the fall, in mid-May, between the 10th and the 13th, I think it was when Jagodnja and Joseva fell, and not a single Muslim entered this Jagodnja and Joseva. And it was my father who entered Joseva, because the Serb forces took him in the direction of Zljebac.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction. I think it's March and not May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. I was going to point that out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So as far as the information we've reviewed is concerned, that information is completely wrong, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll move on to P94. This is -- it seems to be a text file. The title, anyway, is "Srebrenica 73, 1994 Supplement to the ABiH chronicle guide to sector from morale to corps Tuzla." I just want to take you to a couple parts of this document. No page 5 in the English, and in B/C/S page 7, there's reference to the Independent Battalion Biljeg, Territorial Defence Biljeg. Do you see that? Sorry. Page 6. And it's near the bottom "Samostalni bataljon Biljeg i TO Biljeg."

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want you to look at the last -- the sentence at the bottom in Bosnian, where you see 1/6/1992. In English, it says: "On 1/6/1992, the Chetnik attack on Joseva and Jagodnja was rejected."

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask you this: On that date, did anyone from Biljeg help reject a Chetnik attack, as it's described?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There wasn't an attack at Jagodnja and Joseva on the 8th. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, it's the 1st of June, 1st of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no one who came to assist Jagodnja and Joseva on the 1st, and that vehicle didn't go to Zljebac, it went to Jagodnja and Joseva, if that's what you are talking about. I did explain in the course of the attack this vehicle came from the direction of Zljebac, all the way to the centre of Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. So the enemy vehicle was not sabotaged in Zljebac, as this document says?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this information we've just reviewed correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What information do you mean? You mean the bit that we've just read out now? No, no, it's incorrect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Just a few final matters. After Jagodnja and Joseva fell, did you go to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I crossed over when those civilians left, I went in the direction of Srebrenica, with the injured. There were quite a few of them. And then I did not go back to the area, because I had a great deal to do at Srebrenica on a daily basis. I was dressing the wounds of the injured who had come from Jagodnja and Joseva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware when you were in Srebrenica that it had been or was being demilitarised by UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear any stories about the manner in which UNPROFOR soldiers were disarming people?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is this story I heard that in the old town up there, that the UNPROFOR was chasing the Muslims who had arms and that a man jumped off a rock and he got hurt and he was taken to hospital because he had head injury. And that it was impossible to carry weapons around Srebrenica, that there was simply no chance of anyone moving anywhere, going anywhere, in whatever direction, bearing arms.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. You grew up in Jagodnja. Do you know everyone from there?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you say you know everyone from Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd ask if the witness could be shown Exhibit P458, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I'm going to direct you just to two pages of this document. The first is -- it's 03593131, and you should see the date. I think it's the 5th of December, 1992. It says [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see number 16, Osman Salkic, Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the number and there isn't a man under that name at Joseva. This family name does not exist in Joseva, Osman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And then if we turn to another page, which is 03593140. It should say 11 December 1992, the left-hand side -- sorry. It's also handwritten "17" at the top.

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. If you have -- it says 03593140. The left-hand page, Petak, 11 December 1992. There's another list of names, number 8, Hasan Salkic, in Joseva. Again, do you know anyone by that name from Joseva?

utterances.speaker: IBRO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This family name, or that name, actually, don't exist in Joseva.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: And we have a new exhibit I want to pass up. There's no ERN number. And just to explain: This is a census for Joseva. This is a census, and the extract is from Joseva. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document which consists of -- I counted 32 pages. I don't know if anyone else counted with me. utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm very much obliged.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Someone checks me out on the number of pages, because I have -- my fingers are very dry and I am -- I don't quite know whether I managed to count the full 32 of them or ... Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, at this stage, I have no further questions. That's obviously subject to this other issue of which you're all aware.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And I am keeping my fingers crossed, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Well, I know there is some news and there are developments, but I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I [sic] obviously know more than we do. So yes, you may sit down. Mr. Alic -- I think we ought to send Mr. Alic to his room. We need to discuss something before we start the cross-examination, and I don't think you need to be present, because it will only be boring discussion for you on matters that you are not interested in. So what I suggest -- the transcript as Judge Eser rightly points out line 21, I didn't say that "I obviously know more than we do," but that obviously you know more than we do. But that's not a problem. So we'll call you back within a few minutes, hopefully. In the meantime, he can be entertained to a coffee. Thank you. Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I take it that Mr. Di Fazio is going to address the Chamber, or you, Mr. Wubben. I don't know. I mean, I don't know what the arrangements between you are. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, that's so. But I just wonder about what you've got in mind for today's proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I have in mind is precisely -- I can quite understand why you're saying this, but earlier on, I don't -- I think it was Mr. Wubben pointed out that you will be turning up later on. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He also informed us that there was not going to be any reference to any case-law. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then we were specifically asked whether it would be possible to, in conformity with the desire of the Prosecution, that when Mr. Jones finishes his examination-in-chief, we will not consider it finished at all. We will just stay put, remain in limbo until we hear what you have to say. Then, of course, if he wants to proceed any further with his direct, the understanding would be that he would be able to do so. And then he will be followed by cross-examination by Ms. Sellers. That's the understanding. However, if I am not representing what we have discussed and decided earlier on, please tell me. So now, before we go any further. The timing, no, we'll start with the cross-examination for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, do you agree with what I have said, that that is what we agreed earlier on, basically?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Wubben agrees too?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So more or less, we will now want to hear what you have to say. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, it's just a question of when we do this, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think now. MR. DI FAZIO: I've prepared submissions that I can't finish in two minutes or three minutes; that's my point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Well, how long are you going to take? MR. DI FAZIO: Let me propose this: With a kind of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. Oh, I see. You thought that you were going -- we were going to stop at a quarter to 2.00. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. We are going to stop at 2.35. So you've got a full 40 minutes from now. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine. Not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't understand you. MR. DI FAZIO: Fine, fine, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought you were aware of that. MR. DI FAZIO: That explains things and I'm ready to go ahead. Sorry. I didn't understand. I thought we were finishing. Thank you. Your Honours, just some clarifications from yesterday so that the Defence and you know our position. Yesterday I made a submission to you that Annex A, I think it was, one of the annexes, I can't recall precisely which one, did not come --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: B, B. MR. DI FAZIO: B, did not come within the ambit of Rule 68. I will retract that submission. I want to make it clear to you that the Prosecution accepts that it constitutes material that is covered by Rule 68. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just ran out of ink. MR. DI FAZIO: Okay. So before I address that issue and we'll call it the general issue of consequences, can I just give you some background material first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you continue, Mr. Di Fazio, I also got the impression, and I didn't tell you this before, I also got the impression from Mr. Wubben that you are coming back to this courtroom with some additional information on this Slobodan Misic. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And it's precisely because of that that Mr. Wubben tabled his request that we do not consider the direct closed when Mr. Jones sits down. MR. DI FAZIO: That's right. I urged that upon you. You'll understand why when I make -- when I've completed my submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, one of the issues that the Defence raised and have made abundantly clear, they take the view that there must be material documentation resulting from an OTP investigation into this fellow, Mr. Slobodan Misic. On the 8th of December, 1997, a request for assistance was sent to the authorities in the former Yugoslavia requesting an interview with this man. On the 12th of December, 1997, the authorities replied by forwarded to the OTP a document which I'll -- for the sake of simplicity I'll call a -- the Vranje court document. There are copies here; I want to make them available to you. These are being provided this morning to the Defence. And can I ask that I sit down for a moment or two to allow you an opportunity to just quickly go through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. Let's give it a number, an exhibit number. This I haven't got an idea what the next number should be. Madam Registrar. P5 --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P585, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P585. Yes. And P585 consists of two pages in English, purportedly information released to the Tribunal on the case against Slobodan Misic before the district court in Vranje by the Commission for the Collection of Data on crimes against humanity and international law, with reference 02.br.465/97-4 dated 9th December 1997, and signed in Belgrade on the 8th of December, 1997, by Ilija Simic. Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: All right. Yes. Now, if Your Honours will see, the document is in English, there's no ERN number on it. I obtained this from our -- a unit within the Office of the Prosecutor that deals with requests for assistance. This document, as I understand -- I've already made -- asked inquiries to be made to see if this document appears in our computer database anywhere. That inquiry has been made once and I've been informed that it does not. I'm going to make further inquiries this afternoon or cause further inquiries to be made to make absolutely sure. But as I stand here presently advised, I've got good reason to think that this document does not appear in our computer base with ERN numbers and the usual paraphernalia involving it going through the Evidence Unit, MIF forms, and so on. So therefore, it's not accessible to the trial team through normal search material, normal searches conducted on the computer. The material -- document contains material that is Rule 68, and I concede that, and there's a reference to this man killing two prisoners of war, members of the Muslim armed forces, in Bratunac in 1992; again killing seven prisoners of war, members of the Muslim armed forces in Zanjevo; and again, killing further members of the Muslim armed forces in the village of Fakovici in the end of 1992; and more prisoners of war over the Drina River in Bratunac. So the Prosecution concedes that this document is -- contains material that is Rule 68. It's now been handed over to the Defence. I've also -- the Prosecution has also caused inquiries to be made with other team members, to other teams, not team members, not this Prosecution team, but other teams within the Office of the Prosecutor, to see if there were any other inquiries or investigations into this man that they're aware of, and I have been informed that had they are not aware of any ongoing or any past investigations beyond what I've already told you about in that request for assistance back in late 1997. The matter did not, however, end there. The request for assistance was, as I told you, was for an interview with this fellow, Slobodan Misic. Having gone through the RFA file, I found a document in B/C/S that I have not yet had translated. It also does not have ERN numbers and it also was not accessible to the Defence. Madam Vidovic probably has the document now and would know exactly what it says. But the important point I gleaned from it from having it hurriedly translated this morning, before I came into court, note even a draft translation, just the basic gist of it, is that this was a communication to us, the Office of the Prosecutor, that this fellow, Slobodan Misic, did not want to speak to the OTP. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is this document dated? MR. DI FAZIO: I can't see anything that -- there's a fax number on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there's a date on this document, the 12th of December, 1997, where Misic Slobodan declares himself regarding the question of his guilt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you going to tender this document? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I don't know what the attitude of the Defence is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not interested for the time being in the attitude of the Defence. I am only interested in knowing exactly what are the documents you have at your disposal. And if it's not in English, I'm going to ask that it be put on the ELMO or that maybe, I don't know, if Madam Vidovic wants to be -- wants to help us, perhaps she could volunteer to read it out and then it is automatically translated to us into English. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we will know now, like you do, what it says. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. Could it be put on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we could put it on the ELMO. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. And if the interpreters in the booths would be so kind as to interpret it, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know if they accept to do that. I don't think that the interpreters accept to read from the ELMO and translate. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. Very well. Then perhaps Madam Vidovic could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I would still like to see it on the ELMO, because this is not for our eyes only.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies regarding the date. This is what it says: "The minutes were compiled on the 20th of January, 1998, by the investigating judge, pursuant to a request by the Federal Ministry of Justice, dated the 12th of December, 1997." So the document itself was produced on the 20th of January, 1998. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Now, how are we going to overcome this problem of not knowing -- not having a translation and not knowing what this document contains? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I thought that Madam Vidovic was going to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. I mean, I haven't heard Madam Vidovic say, Yes, I'm going to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, by all means, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to show you my appreciation, Ms. Vidovic, for your cooperation. What I suggest is that you try read as slowly as possible, and the appearance of the document itself on the ELMO would help the interpreters follow you better. They have a copy already. Okay. All right. Thank you. So let's proceed. I would suggest you read the document in its entirety, starting from [B/C/S spoken].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, above the word "minutes" or "record," there is the code KI number 59/97. "Records or report compiled on the 20th of January, 1998, by the investigating judge of the district court in Vranje in the criminal case against the accused, Slobodan Misic, from Vranje, for war crimes against the civilian population under Article 142, paragraph 1, and war crimes against prisoners of war, under Article 144 of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia. While the accused pleaded regarding the letter of the Federal Ministry of Justice, 1/1 Number 031/3-1997-04, dated the 12th of December, 1997. Present: Investigating Judge Sloboljub Mihajlovic; clerk, Stojan Milenkovic, recording clerk, Stojan Milenkovic; accused, Slobodan Misic; Defence counsel, Dragan Nikolic, attorney-at-law. Commenced at 12.10 hours. "The accused, Slobodan Misic, was informed about the request of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia sent to the Federal Ministry of Justice, dated the 8th of December, 1997, requesting that the investigators of this Tribunal be allowed to conduct an interview with the accused regarding crimes that he has been charged with. "Furthermore, the accused was informed about the letter of the Federal Ministry of Justice 1/1 Number 031/3-1997, dated the 12th of December, 1997, sent to this investigating judge, requesting that the request be met by the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal unless there are any legal obstacles. "So the accused Slobodan Misic stated as follows: 'I have understood the above request of the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. I hereby state that I do not accept any sort of interview with this Prosecutor, because proceedings are already afoot against me here for crimes that I have been charged with. By the way, I reiterate that I have committed no crime. I was drunk when they took me to the offices of the Vranjski newspaper at Vranje, and I don't know whether they gave me anything to drink there. So I don't know what I told them, nor do I know whether I actually told them what was later printed in the newspapers. One thing I do know is that while volunteering at the front, I killed no civilians or prisoners of war. I have nothing further to state. I recognise the record as accurately reflecting my own statement and hereby sign the statement,'" completed at 1230, the accused. You have the signature of the recording clerk on one side of the page, the signature of the investigating judge on the other, and there is the stamp of the district court in Vranje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Madam Vidovic. Yes. And do you wish to address the Trial Chamber further on this document, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: Well, only that it illustrates to you why there was no investigation. So the history of what I've told you, that I obtained from the RFA unit, and the two documents that have been tendered, incidentally, if Your Honour pleases, I do seek to tender this, so it will show why there is very little material that the Prosecution -- or this Prosecution team was able to uncover in respect of any such investigation. A, no investigation, and B, these documents stayed in someone else's office and were not ERN'd and not normally accessible to those conducting normal, diligent, responsible searches for documentation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it from what you've said that the Office of the Prosecutor is not in a position to provide this Trial Chamber with any information as to the outcome of the proceedings that were instituted in Serbia against Slobodan Misic? MR. DI FAZIO: That I can't tell you. I don't know the answer to that question. If Your Honours are interested in that, I can make -- cause inquiries to be made and try and get whatever information we have about the outcome of matters in the former Yugoslavia, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not a question of the Trial Chamber being interested. What we are interested in knowing is whether, because of the fact that this Mr. Misic decided not to cooperate with the Tribunal, in other words, decided not to release any statements or be interviewed by any officer of the Tribunal, then, consequently, the Tribunal lost -- the Office of the Prosecutor of this Tribunal lost interest in him to the extent that it did not pursue its investigations to the extent of at least following the proceedings that were ongoing against the gentleman in Serbia. This is what I want to know. And otherwise, the Trial Chamber itself is not interested in having -- I mean, we are not a party to this case. MR. DI FAZIO: My inquiries to date, the ones that I've told you about, the inquiries conducted with other trial teams in the Office of the Prosecutor, all have indicated that there was no further investigation. I will again, as I said, ask for confirmation of what I have been told, and I'll look into that this afternoon. But that's my -- as I stand here, that is how I'm currently advised. That's what the situation is. This brought an end to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Di Fazio, for all that information. Can I have that document, please, the one that Madam Usher put on the ELMO. MR. DI FAZIO: And I thank Madam Vidovic for having read out the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this document that we've just been dealing with, consisting of one page, with reference number Ki.br.59/97.- and having at the top a telephone number and the words "ICTY Belgrade" has been tendered and received and marked as Prosecution Exhibit P586. I don't know, Mr. Jones, if you have -- I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I thought you had finished. Sorry. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. MR. DI FAZIO: I haven't finished, if Your Honours please. I intend to make the bulk of my submissions today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yeah. Then let's -- how long? How much more do you require? MR. DI FAZIO: I'll finish by 2.35. There's no question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. But we have a witness here who is waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I'd also like to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, of course. No, but you will have -- I mean, please, don't for a moment even think that we are going to dispose of this without looking at you and asking you for your -- in fact, I had already tried to do that, not realising that he hadn't finished. But I think we -- you want to wait for a moment, Mr. Di Fazio. Please sit down. Usher, get the witness in again and I'll explain to him why we are sending him back. And do you still think you would be able to finish tomorrow, Ms. Sellers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SELLERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes, I will be able to finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: What I -- while he's coming, what I rather had in mind, I thought that I was going to -- was going to happen, the suggestion that I had, was that I go as far as I can because there's -- today, and there's more inquiry that I want to make. Now, I'm hoping that that will all be finished by the end of the day, and any more material that I've gathered will be sent to the Defence tonight. So what I was going to suggest is I finish my submissions today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. We are going to give you all that opportunity. This is it. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes. And then I can get whatever new material I can to the Defence this afternoon. They will have an opportunity to read it, and then they can make their minds up on whether to pursue anything further with the witness and reply tomorrow. That's what I respectfully suggest might be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, good afternoon to you again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told you before I sent you back to your room that we had something to discuss, and unfortunately I was wrong. I thought we were going to deal and finish with the issue that we needed to discuss, which does not concern you, in a matter of a few minutes. Unfortunately, it got more complicated than that. We need much more than a few minutes to discuss and decide on this other issue which is beside -- hasn't got to do with you. And I thought it would be better, rather than keeping you waiting and then maybe testifying for five minutes or ten minutes, to send you back to your hotel and so that you can have lunch and rest, and then you will return back tomorrow morning. Tomorrow morning, if we are lucky and everything goes well, we should finish with your testimony. So my apologies to you, but at the same time, I think it's better to go back to your hotel rather than stay waiting in a small room here, not knowing if you're going to continue to give evidence today or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would be extremely grateful if we were able to finish up tomorrow, because I have a disabled mother back in Bosnia and, therefore, staying away is very difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will do -- I can assure you that we will do our utmost. And if we don't finish tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if we don't finish tomorrow, we will certainly finish early on Friday. So you can put your mind at rest that you will be back home this weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. So that's the result of our inquiries into the investigation that the Defence raised in its motion, the issue of the Prosecution investigation into this fellow. In addition to that, yesterday the Prosecution asked that electronic searches be conducted of its database for this man, this Slobodan Misic. That was being conducted yesterday by one of the -- one of our team, and last night I asked that it be expanded and that it be sent to the ISU, that's our professional searching department, so to speak, for a far more refined and broader search. And that's under way, and it's being completed. And the material has been produced, and it's not huge. It's not voluminous. And I'll be able to get through it, I hope, with the assistance of one or two of my colleagues, this afternoon, and be in a position to hand on anything that is thrown out over to the Defence regarding this man. So that would then mean that they should have the material tonight and be in a position to know if they want to make any use of it with this particular witness. So they are the inquiries that the Prosecution has undertaken. They're incomplete, as I said, and the main -- the area that needs to be attended to is the actual review of what the computer generated for us. So I want to turn, if I may, briefly, to the issue of prejudice, and there's something that's come up today as a result of what's in P586 that I would like to have a closer look at and consider, and I would not like to complete any submissions that I make on the issue of prejudice to you until I've had a chance to consider P586. So can I reserve this -- on this issue until tomorrow? I understand one of the -- I understand that one of either Annex A or C is in evidence, if not both of them. I don't know the exhibit numbers, but I understand that they were tendered yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. They were tendered today. MR. DI FAZIO: Today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or one was tendered yesterday, I think, and one was tendered today. That's how it would stand. What was Annex A was tendered yesterday. What is Annex B or C was tendered today. MR. DI FAZIO: So they've both gone into evidence. I know that that is not a complete answer to the issue of prejudice, and I don't pretend that it is, but the fact remains that the evidence is now before the Trial Chamber and the Defence can make whatever use it can, even at this late stage, of the document. So the Prosecution's submission is that their prejudice has been mitigated. The extent to which it's been mitigated is, of course, a matter for you. I know that the -- immediately what Mr. Jones would say, or perhaps you, Your Honours, would say is that it doesn't accommodate -- it doesn't take care of the fact that the Defence were thereby deprived of putting the document to the Prosecution witnesses. I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the whole issue. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, it's -- the Prosecution's submission is it's a large part of the issue, but not the whole issue. And I say that it's not the whole issue partly because of the fact that it's now at least in front of the Trial Chamber and something that you -- and that they can make use of. I've not reviewed every Prosecution witness who might have mentioned Fakovici, but I've reviewed what I think are the principal witnesses who come from the area, Prosecution witnesses, that is. All of them testified that -- well, Novka Bozic -- perhaps I shouldn't use names. One of the witnesses testified that she didn't see any VRS in her village, and the basic thrust of her evidence was that the only armed units or military presence in the village were the men in her village and she basically described a village guard. And that's around page 1324, 1348 of the transcript. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO: I won't refer to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's a safer approach. MR. DI FAZIO: A Divovici witness - let's put it that way - you'll find her evidence, that's a lady, at page 1383, parts that I'm referring to, also testified about the presence of a village guard and no military presence. And as far as the other material in the document is concerned, she said that there were no Muslims in Zanjevo who were driven away, and there's reference, I think, in one, either A or C, to that. And also she described the presence of a village guard. Another gentleman, he -- you'll find his evidence at least at page 1523, said that there wasn't a single unit - and I understand him to be talking about a VRS -- or military unit I should say, military unit in Fakovici in May of 1992. He agreed with the general proposition that there was SDS arming through a gentleman named Slavko Jovanovic in the Fakovici area. And he denied coordination between the JNA and certain people. I think that's the expression in the transcript, "certain people," from Serbia, page 1524. Another witness who spoke about the matter was a gentleman you'll find parts of his evidence at page 3167. He again -- the thrust of his evidence was village guard, there were stored weapons there. He agreed there were stored weapons in the post office, I think it was, in Fakovici - I think Ms. Richardson talked to that witness - distributed only to locals and, again, Muslims not forced to leave Zanjevo. And all parties participated in the arming of local populations. I don't need to go through it in much more detail. The two insider witnesses, the doctor, you'll recall, and the other gentleman, policeman, who I took in examination-in-chief -- in -- whose evidence I took, didn't, as far as I understand, my view of their evidence, make much or say much about the presence of paramilitaries or types like Slobodan Misic in the Fakovici area or in the broader area. Now, the reason I say that is that I know that you -- I cannot stand here and say to you we know -- we know for sure what they would have said had Defence counsel put those documents to them. But it's not silly to say that they -- it's likely, given the state of their evidence, that they would have denied any such knowledge of any such events and that, therefore, the Prosecution -- sorry, the Defence would be likely to be in a position of having their evidence, but having the document in evidence and being able to make the usual submissions to you that they -- that you would expect from them. So that's something that you may care to consider in the exercise of your discretion. I don't know if the point has appealed to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you look at my face, you would know, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Very well. But one thing's for sure, that the prejudice must be mitigated to some extent, to some extent at least, by the fact that you've got the document in front of you and the Defence has now access to it and can make whatever use of it it sees fit. So that's what I want to say today about the use of A and C, Annexes A and C. As I said, there's another matter that I may care to raise tomorrow. I'd like to do that after I've looked at Exhibit P586 and considered its impact on the issue of prejudice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 586. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry. Yes, 586 is the one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. 586. It doesn't seem on the face of the document that the person concerned, Misic, Slobodan Misic, is retracting anything except as regards his alleged killing of several persons. Otherwise he is not retracting anything else. He's only retracting his responsibility for the alleged murders. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, he said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So he is not retracting that the -- his participation in combat in the region or his being a volunteer, a volunteer from Serbia. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: But it's not all that he said, and there are other matters and I'd like to have a chance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, and you will have the opportunity. MR. DI FAZIO: Yesterday -- that's the only matter I make at this stage that I'm likely to come back to you on tomorrow, and that will be very, very brief, if at all. The basic thrust of the submissions made by Mr. Jones yesterday was that there's a systematic failure here, that this is what you're dealing with here, because of our failure to hand over this Rule 68 material to the Defence. There was a complaint that by the Prosecution raising the issue of whether or not we would avail ourselves of any argument based on the fact that the documents might or might not be in the public domain evidences an attitude on the part of the Prosecution that it wishes to wriggle out of or not accept its responsibilities to twist and turn, so to speak. Those inquiries that I told you about earlier were under way yesterday, if Your Honours please. There is nothing wrong with the Prosecution availing itself of a proper argument if it's open to it. If, indeed, these documents had been, or if the Prosecution considered that it was in a position to argue with you, to make -- sorry, to make a submission to you that documents are in the public domain and therefore are absolved of any responsibility under Rule 68, then it would have been negligent on our part not to do so. So far from twisting and turning, as the Defence would have you believe, the Prosecution was attempting to deal with the very issues that were concerning the Defence yesterday. If Your Honours please, another matter that you should bear in mind regarding any systematic failure, such -- and of course, to invoke the Rule 68 bis provision that you have, any sanction - is this: On the 19th of May last year, we obtained search results from the ISU section or unit, call it what you will, and it -- we had sent various criteria to them to use in order to research what material was available to them on the -- on our database, and they came back with a large swathe of documents. One of the documents was this document, either A or C, I can't recall, the excerpts from the newspaper Odgovor Bumerang. It was described in the spreadsheet that we received as back in May of 2004. Yes. Thank you, it's A. It was described as the excerpts from newspaper Odgovor Bumerang, including interview with Slobodan Misic, aka Top, Serb volunteer, page 4. So the searches that we did, and there were many, many, many more searches than that one, produced the document that is Rule 68. The failure, therefore, must have occurred at some point thereafter. And I don't know what caused the failure. I don't know, and I don't think -- well, no one in the team knows if it was caused by someone looking at the document and saying, Well, it's not Rule 68, or whether it wasn't considered at all. Either one is a mistake and it's a bad mistake, and the Prosecution doesn't shrink from that. And I can't tell you which -- what happened, because I just don't know. I can't figure out from the material that we have what happened. But the fact is that the system did give us the document. It's human error that's led to this one or two documents that should have been given to the Defence. So if you accept what I've said about the system that the Prosecution has been using, and if you accept the arguments that I've put to you relating to the search that was conducted last year, then what you're dealing with here is the failure of -- the human failure of someone in the trial team at some point either overlooked it or made a bad assessment about the document, that it wasn't discloseable. But the system itself is working, and since last year I think we've had -- this is the second major occasion in which this sort of issue has arisen. You'll recall last year I was standing making submissions about Andjelko Makar, the statement from Andjelko Makar. We deal with hundreds of thousands of documents, if Your Honours please. It's important, I know, that the Defence get this sort of material, but I submit to you that if all indications are that this is an isolated example that doesn't warrant the -- invoking powers under Rule 68 bis and/or exercising discretion to sanction the Prosecution. So that's all I want to say about the matters, if Your Honours please, other than anything I might add to you in relation -- arising from P586.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Jones, we've only got six minutes. I take it that you would require more than that. I don't know. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Both my colleague and I want to raise a couple of matters, very important matters, in relation to this documents. I certainly could make a few points now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you can utilise the next six minutes, I think that would be worth its while. But otherwise, if you feel uncomfortable about it and would rather start and continue, then we can start tomorrow. It's up to you. I mean, I'm leaving you the choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: I think if we can start now and then we can finish tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My colleague will add a couple of observations at a certain point. Your Honour, firstly, this new document, which has been produced today, in our submission, raises far more questions than it answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which one are you referring to? 585 or 586?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: My apologies. I didn't -- 585, P585. It's a document from the Commission for the Collection of Data on crimes against humanity, international law. It's essentially a summary of information. It's not from the court. It's not from the investigating judge. It's not the dossier. And in this document, it's apparent that actually investigations were carried out to the extent that in fact seven witnesses were heard who were together with Misic at the front in Mladenici and in the region of Fakovici. So here are seven people who spoke to an investigating judge and who were in this area of direct concern to us with Misic. And it reads on: "Their testimonies indicate that Misic was indeed present at both fronts and that he participated in some of the clashes, but not in the mopping-up operations." So already we have corroboration that Misic was there in the area, participating in clashes. These witness statements are obviously also of great interest to us. The testimonies also indicate that he could not have committed the murders he had been talking about, although specific enumerated murders, it's not anything more than that. However, it does go on to say: "It was mentioned during these testimonies that he cut off the head of the corpse of a Muslim and put it on a fence in the vicinity of Fakovici." So in other words, those testimonies actually corroborate one of the atrocities, and that's certainly a war crime as well, defacing a body. So we have a court file, which must exist. We have the statements of seven witnesses. We saw in the other documents, D833, which we exhibited today, that in fact the State Security Service seized tapes of the interview with Misic and Misic's authorised transcript. Now, certainly the Prosecution has a duty to investigate war crimes, certainly war crimes of this gravity, and I submit it's simply extraordinary to suspect that the Prosecution, on receiving information -- not information, on hearing from the person who has confessed to these crimes that he was drunk and later attempt to retract it, that that would be sufficient, that that would close the matter, as if any investigating authority in the world would hear a murderer make confessions; and then when he says, Well, I was drunk, I didn't do it, would say, That's all right then, we needn't look into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's precisely what I pointed out early on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes. Impossible. I submit that if it is true, then it's staggering that that's -- that the Prosecutor of this Tribunal, with its solemn duty to investigate crimes of this seriousness would simply shrug off such gross crimes and not investigate further. Now Moreover, this document is by no way final. It says at the end: "The investigation continues." So it's inconclusive, firstly. And secondly, let's bear in mind with the date, 1997, and this is from Belgrade, that it's well documented, it's a matter of public records from the looks of the annual reports of this Tribunal, certainly at that time, Serbia and Montenegro, Yugoslavia, was well-known for not taking seriously its duty to prosecute crimes of an international concern. In fact, I indeed in fact went with the President of this Tribunal to Belgrade on a trip around this time to try and persuade the authorities to arrest the Vukovar 3 and to take some action because there was a culture of complete impunity in Serbia at that time. So again, if even the court in Serbia had closed the investigation hurriedly, now that certainly should not be something which should have satisfied the Prosecution of this Tribunal that there was nothing in it. In any event, we don't even have that information that the investigation didn't go further. Moreover, it emerges from this that this individual has a criminal record, was a violent personality. It's obviously clearly of relevance that he was in the area with that background, and the fact that he was drinking -- no doubt if we had committed serious crimes, murder of civilians, one might take to the bottle as well. I can't believe that that was in any way considered a reason for not looking further into the matter. And the second document is simply Misic indicating that he didn't want to speak to the Prosecutor. Obviously, I don't see how that would end matters when you have corroborating witness statements and the duty of the Prosecutor to inquire into these matters. And it's also contradictory with P585, because in P585, it's stated that Misic used his right to remain silent, whereas in P586, in fact he's speaking and denying the commission of certain crimes. So again, that's why I say, it raises more questions than it answers, because obviously a lot more has been said. And even in the two exhibits which we -- two documents which we exhibited, one could see that there were two different -- different stories, but a story about snakes, the rather lurid story about snakes, was not in the first document. Clearly Misic did not simply give one interview in which he said a few things. It's been reported in quite a few different journals and different things being reported. So again, I would find it extraordinary if the Prosecutor hadn't looked into this more and if there weren't more material disclosed to us. Now, Your Honours, the point I wanted to make yesterday when the Prosecution was beginning to look into this is that it's standard response that, Well, we've got millions of documents to search through. But here in these documents, we have names of individuals: The spokesperson of this Tribunal, a woman in Belgrade. I won't mention names, so as not to embarrass them. But surely it's a matter of speaking to those people; speaking to the former deputy Prosecutor; speaking to senior trial attorneys; contacting the Helsinki Commission, which had expressed an interest in the case; and the institutional knowledge of the Prosecution which is available and which has to be called upon to find out whether anything was done. And certainly, if those things haven't been done - and then we'll undertake that ourselves. We'll speak to the spokesperson, who is still at this Tribunal, and others, and if there is a lot more out there, then we'll certainly bring that to your attention. Now, the Prosecution's response, their standard response, it seems, in this situation is to say there's no prejudice. It's hard for us to imagine what the Prosecution would consider prejudice. But Your Honours will have seen how, particularly in this case, we've already tendered 830 or something exhibits. And they are carefully interlocked. And you will have seen with Slobodan Misic, we found his name on another list and we can link the name on that list with another document. And there's the enormous prejudice of being a year into the trial and not having had documents which we could have analysed and seen the interconnections and then put to Prosecution witnesses. Now, as far as those witnesses are concerned, we say, and we've always said, that those witnesses, when they speak of village guards and they deny ethnic cleansing by Serbs, are deeply biased. Make no bones about it. That's our characters and that that bias runs through their testimony against our client. Nonetheless, who is to say whether these witnesses are so, in our submission, biased that if presented with a document of this impact, that they might not actually recall some terrible incident mentioned there and say, Well, in fact it's true, I can't deny it, there were terrible things which the Serbs were doing in Zanjevo or wherever. And we could have got through this implacable denial of some of the witnesses with this document, possibly. As for the insiders, the notion that the doctor and the other witness would not have in fact expanded upon the events described in these documents is a matter which Your Honours can judge, but certainly the insider witnesses had plenty to say which was of interest in favour of us, as they did for the Prosecution, as I'm sure you'll recall. And they certainly could have expanded on the information in these documents. So I should perhaps stop there so that my colleague can continue either today or tomorrow. But as I say, the prejudice consists of being deprived of exculpatory material for a year which we could have investigated and analysed. And certainly we say it's considerable and we do say it's a systematic failure as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's continue tomorrow, Mr. Jones. I'm sorry to have to interrupt you here, but I don't want to keep anyone else beyond the time that much further beyond the time that we agreed upon. We will resume tomorrow morning at 9.00 in courtroom -- here? In this unfortunate courtroom, yes. Ms. Vidovic, can you postpone until tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can, Your Honour. I just want to say two or three things that might make the Prosecutor's work easier. There's something I've noticed concerning these documents, especially the latter, concerns their authenticity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you discuss it when we stop? At least the recorder doesn't need to continue typing.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, not with the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then we'll continue tomorrow, because, honestly, I will have complaints if I continue with the sitting beyond here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 20th day of October, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24 25
